prompt.context: We have been contacted by a large distilled spirits manufacturing and marketing company to develop a new strategy for one of their brands. The brand competes only in the premium scotch segment and holds 25% market share of volume (tied #2 with another brand; #1 has 35%). The brand is priced about 10% above the industry average. The scotch industry has declined in volume every year since the 1960s at roughly 3% per year through 1996, then slowed to 1% per year in 1996-1998.
prompt.question: How would you develop a new strategy for this scotch brand, and what strategic recommendation would you make?

clarifying_info.q: How is the scotch market segmented?
clarifying_info.a: Three segments: low-end (~40% of volume, ~20% of profit), premium (~50% of volume, ~60% of profit), super-premium (~10% of volume, ~20% of profit).

clarifying_info.q: Why has scotch volume been declining?
clarifying_info.a: Fewer people are drinking scotch. Two reasons: a general popularity decline (vodka and wine have grown), and a shrinking of the 35-50 age demographic that traditionally drinks scotch. However, baby boomers are now aging into that segment, so the demographic pressure may ease going forward.

clarifying_info.q: What are the key customer needs in scotch?
clarifying_info.a: Taste (actual or perceived), fashion (is it trendy to drink), and badge value (does it make me feel sophisticated/mature/important).

clarifying_info.q: How does the brand compare to competitors on key attributes?
clarifying_info.a: The brand has disadvantaged taste and badge relative to competitors, but competitive fashion. Distribution is actually advantaged. Advertising awareness is fine, but advertising effectiveness is poor — consumers remember ads but are not convinced to buy.

clarifying_info.q: What does the competitive set look like?
clarifying_info.a: #1 brand has 35% share and has been gaining share mostly from our brand. #2 is tied with us at 25% and has held share. #4 has 10%, others 5%. #1 spends the most on selling and advertising costs and commands a 10% price premium. #2 is at the industry average price.

clarifying_info.q: What is wrong with the advertising?
clarifying_info.a: The brand spends about 25% too little, spends heavily on cheap billboards that reach the wrong audiences, over-indexes at Christmas capturing only impulse buyers, and has had poor creative campaigns versus #1's very effective campaigns.

clarifying_info.q: Is this brand important to the parent company?
clarifying_info.a: No — it is only a small part of the company's overall portfolio.

framework: 1. Define strategy (Participation, Offering, Pricing, Operating Configuration, Distribution)
2. Position Assessment — understand profitability drivers, market economics, and competitive position
3. Industry analysis — size, segmentation, profit pool, structural attractiveness (Porter's Five Forces)
4. Brand diagnosis — share trends, relative attributes (taste, badge, fashion), pricing, distribution, advertising
5. Alternative identification — enumerate strategic options for the brand
6. Alternative evaluation — assess profit potential and implementability of each option
7. Recommendation — choose the best path with risks and next steps

questions.guidance: A strong answer covers the key dimensions of strategy: where to participate (geography, customer, product segment), what to offer (product, service), how to price, how to configure operations (cost/asset base), and how to distribute. Avoid a vague one-liner.

questions.prompt: What is your process to develop a new strategy?
questions.guidance: Position Assessment (business profitability, existing strategies, market economics, competitive position) → Alternative Identification → Alternative Evaluation → Business Plan. Candidate should show a structured hypothesis-driven approach.

questions.prompt: What do you want to know in the first scoping meeting with the client?
questions.guidance: Key items: any political or ulterior motives, prior work done on the subject, what the client wants to learn, how they want to work together, time constraints, who should be involved, basic brand data (profit, volume), any existing hypotheses, likely alternatives already on the table, and non-negotiable questions.

questions.prompt: What might make you NOT want to accept this project?
questions.guidance: Red flags include: internal politics that undermine honest work, client not committed to acting on findings, client looking for a scapegoat, an unmanageable business-unit stakeholder, or the client being generally difficult to work with.

questions.prompt: What caused the steady volume decline through 1996, the 'kink' to only 1% decline in 1996-1998, and what will likely happen going forward?
questions.guidance: Decline driven by fewer people drinking scotch (not less consumption per drinker). Two causes: general popularity loss to vodka/wine, and shrinkage of the 35-50 core demographic. The kink reflects the baby boomer cohort beginning to age into the 35-50 segment, partially offsetting the popularity decline. Going forward, continued demographic tailwind from boomers plus a growing interest in single malts and super-premium scotch suggests the rate of decline may slow further or stabilize.

questions.prompt: Is the scotch industry structurally profitable? Explain using a framework.
questions.guidance: Yes, highly profitable despite volume decline. Key structural factors: high barriers to entry (brand establishment takes decades), strong brand loyalty reducing customer switching, taste acquisition barrier limits new drinkers, low price sensitivity, high regulatory/tax burden deters entrants, and moderate (not intense) competitive rivalry with limited price wars. Net result: strong margins, but profits erode as total volume falls.

questions.prompt: Where is the profit concentrated in the market, and what does this imply?
questions.guidance: Volume: low-end 40%, premium 50%, super-premium 10%. Profit: low-end 20%, premium 60%, super-premium 20%. Premium is the most attractive segment per unit of volume. Super-premium punches above its volume weight. The client's brand is in premium, which is correct from a profit standpoint.

questions.prompt: What hypotheses would you test to explain the brand's relative underperformance (losing share to #1)?
questions.guidance: Key hypotheses and findings: (1) Disadvantaged taste and badge attributes vs. competitors — TRUE. (2) Distribution gap — FALSE, distribution is actually advantaged. (3) Overpriced relative to attributes — TRUE. (4) Low advertising awareness — FALSE, awareness is fine. (5) Poor advertising effectiveness — TRUE, consumers remember ads but are not persuaded to buy.

questions.prompt: Why has advertising effectiveness been poor, and how should the advertising budget be set?
questions.guidance: Four problems: (1) Under-spending by ~25%, (2) wrong media mix (too much billboard, not enough targeted media), (3) wrong timing (Christmas impulse focus misses brand-loyal buyers), (4) poor creative vs. #1's strong campaigns. Budget-setting approaches: reach/frequency build-back; match competitor spend (requires ~100% increase); match competitor % of revenue; index spend to desired price premium (e.g., #1 spends $10M for 10% premium; if we want 0% premium we'd spend industry average ~$5M); break-even analysis.

math.setup: Industry average ad spend = $5MM/year. #1 brand has 10% price premium and spends $10MM/year (double industry average). To match #1's spend would require a 100% increase from current levels. Alternatively, index: desired price premium / #1 price premium × #1 spend = implied spend.
steps: #1 ad spend index: $10MM for 10% price premium = $1MM per 1% premium point
Current brand targets 10% price premium, so implied spend = $10MM (match #1)
That is a 100% increase over current spending
If brand were to drop to 0% price premium, implied spend = $5MM (industry average)
If brand were to price 10% below average, implied spend = $2.5MM (half industry average)
math.answer: Matching #1 requires roughly doubling the current advertising budget.

questions.prompt: If the goal is to maximize profit (not necessarily share), what are the strategic alternatives?
questions.guidance: Full list of alternatives: (1) Reformulate product to improve taste/badge attributes, (2) change pricing (reduce premium to match attributes), (3) reduce costs, (4) change distribution, (5) change advertising/promotion strategy, (6) sell the brand, (7) milk the brand (harvest cash, minimize investment). Candidate should generate this list before evaluating.

questions.prompt: Which alternative offers the greatest profit potential?
questions.guidance: Best profit alternatives are 'milk the brand' or 'sell the brand.' Rationale: market volume is declining so steeply that any advertising or investment to turn around the brand will likely never be recovered. Brand value also erodes over time as volume falls, making a sale attractive sooner rather than later. A third option — invest to rebuild the entire scotch category (e.g., coordinating with other producers, linking scotch to cigars/fashion trends) — has merit but is harder to execute unilaterally.

questions.prompt: Which alternative will be easiest to implement?
questions.guidance: Consider: Is this the company's flagship brand? (No — small part of portfolio, so milking or selling does not threaten the parent.) Does the strategy fit the rest of the portfolio? (If all other brands are growth brands, milking one is easier to manage.) Will management attention on this brand crowd out other brands? These filters reinforce the milk/sell recommendation.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential strategic alternatives for a premium scotch brand that is losing share in a declining market?

categories.name: Product
ideas: Reformulate scotch to improve perceived taste
Develop new packaging to strengthen badge value
Launch a super-premium or single-malt extension

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Reduce price premium to align with current attribute ratings
Price at industry average to compete head-to-head with #2
Introduce tiered pricing across sub-brands

categories.name: Advertising & Marketing
ideas: Double advertising spend to match #1
Shift media mix away from billboards to targeted channels
Spread spend throughout the year, not just Christmas
Overhaul creative to improve purchase persuasion
Link brand to fashionable lifestyle trends (e.g., cigars, cocktail culture)

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: Leverage advantaged distribution for promotional programs
Increase on-premise (bar/restaurant) visibility
Partner with high-end venues to strengthen badge

categories.name: Portfolio / Corporate
ideas: Milk the brand: cut investment, harvest cash flow
Sell the brand while it still has value
Coordinate with other industry players on category-building advertising

categories.name: Category Growth
ideas: Convince other producers to invest collectively in growing the scotch category
Target new demographics (younger consumers, women)
Position scotch as the premium alternative to wine/vodka

recommendation: Recommend milking the brand in the near term: cut advertising and sales investment to minimum sustaining levels and harvest cash flow.

If the parent company does not want to manage a declining asset, sell the brand promptly while it retains meaningful market share (25%) and brand equity, before further volume erosion reduces its value.

Do not invest heavily to turn around the brand — the declining market makes it nearly impossible to recover the required advertising investment, and the brand's attribute disadvantages (taste, badge) require costly and uncertain remediation.
risks: Milking accelerates share loss, which could make a future sale harder or reduce sale price
Competitor #1 may use this brand's withdrawal of advertising to consolidate the premium segment further
If the scotch category reverses its decline faster than expected (due to baby boomer demographics and single-malt trends), the brand will have forfeited upside
next_steps: Quantify the NPV of milking vs. selling under different volume-decline scenarios
Commission a brand valuation to establish a sale price floor
Evaluate whether category-building coordination with other producers is feasible before committing to harvest/exit
Review whether any super-premium extension could be carved out and retained if the premium brand is sold
